title: T300 Printer Project Sign-off Home
summary: Owner sign-off entry point for the T300 firmware, safety, slicing, and commissioning work.

work.nextAction: Prove recovery boot and capture the full eMMC image before any printer write.

content.text: Plain summary

The printer has not been migrated yet. The physical T300 is still on the restorable Comgrow/Sovol 1.5.2 image with patched Klipper 0.12.0. The repository now contains the v14 commissioning-locked mainline candidate, recovery tooling, safety policy, portable Orca 2.4.2 profiles, editable review projects, and validation tests.

My recommendation is to treat the current repository state as ready for the final attended recovery-media update and backup work, not ready for installation. The USB image and boot files verify correctly, but one explicit Klipad50 device-tree setting and the refreshed recovery safety overlay are still staged on the laptop rather than written to the stick. After that owner-approved update, the next real-world gate is proving three recovery boots and capturing the full eMMC backup before any printer write. Orca is already staged on this laptop, but the first-layer test, bracket, and Frieren remain editable projects until commissioning and their required filament calibrations are accepted.
What changed in the project
A pinned mainline stack was prepared around Klipper v0.13.0, Moonraker, Mainsail, KlipperScreen, Crowsnest, KAMP line purge, and a bounded timelapse service.
Safety is moved out of fragile slicer start G-code and into a policy layer, an admission scanner, and reviewed lifecycle macros.

attrs.title: Review g-code safety layer
attrs.instruction:
explain to me why g-code is a fragile place for safety and if moving this layer somewhere different has any downsides.  

I have concerns that since g-code is something produced by slicers the slicers will be expecting these safety features in this layer. is that something we have accounted for?
attrs.resolution: Answered in this page: slicer G-code remains the print recipe, while reusable hardware protection lives in Klipper, the admission scanner, and bounded lifecycle macros. The downside is a stricter Orca/profile contract and fewer arbitrary files accepted.

content.text: The OrcaSlicer profile now emits a small contract: object definitions, START_PRINT temperatures, END_PRINT, pause, M600, and optional per-layer timelapse frames.
The Dossier Engine clone is downstream-only on this laptop: it fetches updates, and its push URL is disabled.

The public printer repository contains only redistributable code, profiles, tests, and documentation. Purchased GerGo material, recovery images, credentials, and generated owner-specific stages remain ignored and local.
Why safety is not mainly in slicer G-code

G-code is the recipe for one print. OrcaSlicer generates it, a person can edit it, an old file can sit on a USB stick for months, and a different slicer can produce a different startup style. That makes G-code a poor place for rules that must protect the printer every single time.

The slicer can request heat, speed, fan output, object labels, and macro calls, but it cannot see live sensor failures, MCU communication loss, probe faults, or whether Klipper is blocked inside a home, probe, or temperature wait.
A stale or wrong slicer profile could omit cleanup, call the wrong startup macro, include an old factory corner purge, or home at the wrong time.
Per-file safety is duplicated safety. Every G-code file becomes another copy that might be outdated, hand-edited, or made for another firmware.
Normal G-code runs through Klipper's queued command path. Emergency stop, heater verification, endstop/probe handling, and MCU watchdog behavior must remain below that queue.

Moving safety lower does have downsides. The printer accepts fewer arbitrary files, the Orca profile has to follow the reviewed contract, and third-party G-code may need to be re-sliced or rejected instead of merely warned about. A bug in the shared policy could also affect all prints, which is why it is tested separately and kept small.

The design accounts for what slicers expect by keeping Orca responsible for model geometry, per-move paths, ordinary print speeds, temperatures within policy, fan commands, flow percentages, object labels, filament-change calls, and optional layer timelapse calls. The printer owns homing, mesh creation, purge placement, the build-plate rearm gate, startup order, end/cancel parking, and hard ceilings. In plain terms: Orca describes what to print; the printer decides whether that recipe is safe to run on this T300.
Current refinement candidate

The refinement safely supports Orca's per-filament pressure advance during an admitted print. Values must be finite and between 0 and 0.20. Smooth-time changes, alternate extruders, unknown parameters, values before START_PRINT, and uploaded TUNING_TOWER commands are refused. Startup and every cleanup path reset pressure advance to zero. A paused admitted print may perform only that zero reset, allowing cancellation to finish without allowing paused tuning changes.

The old generic 5 mm stationary-extrusion allowance is gone. A stationary positive move can only return filament that the same print previously retracted. Tiny, capped allowances cover Orca 2.4.2 decimal rounding without creating a usable stationary purge allowance. A stage-bound 900-layer digital job near the T300 build limits passed with 36,000 retract/wipe recoveries, while repeated stationary and microscopic-move allowance farming was rejected.

Mainsail and KlipperScreen gain a read-only Printer Status action. Its internal macro command is T_STATUS because exact Klipper v0.13 rejects macro names containing digits; the visible human label remains Printer Status. It reports temperatures, homing, plate readiness, commissioning lock, and filament-sensor state without moving or heating anything.

Four editable Orca review projects are staged in Downloads/T300-Orca-Review-20260805: the standard first-layer test, orange camera bracket, Frieren quality candidate, and Frieren easier-support-release candidate. They deliberately contain no final G-code. Orca still needs conservative placeholder values to open and preview a project, but those profiles are visibly CALIBRATION REQUIRED and no pressure-advance, flow, temperature, volumetric-speed, or retraction result is treated as accepted.
Sign-off position

Approve the design direction if you agree with the priorities: hardware safety first, reversible recovery first, no hidden firmware updates, no private GerGo redistribution, no hand-edited model meshes, and no printer movement or heat initiated by automation without you physically choosing it.
Do not approve physical installation yet unless the recovery checklist, image backup, boot identity checks, and attended commissioning steps are completed in order.
